title: The Tyranny of the Number
text:
Modern institutions love to measure. Hospitals are judged by waiting times, schools by examination results, police forces by reported crime and government departments by targets met. The appeal is obvious: numbers seem objective, they allow comparison, and they promise to hold the powerful to account. Yet a growing body of experience suggests that when a measure becomes a target, it often ceases to measure what it was meant to.

The problem is not that numbers are false but that people respond to them. A hospital told to reduce the time patients spend waiting in its emergency department may find ways of moving them onto trolleys in corridors, where the clock no longer runs. A school judged solely by pass rates may discourage weaker pupils from sitting examinations at all. In each case the figure improves while the reality it was supposed to reflect stays the same or grows worse. Energy that should go into the work goes into managing the measurement.

There is a subtler cost as well. What is easily counted tends to crowd out what is not. The kindness of a nurse, the curiosity a good teacher awakens, the trust a police officer builds in a neighbourhood: none of these appears in a performance table, and in institutions that value only what appears there, they are gradually neglected. Professionals who once took pride in their judgement come to feel that they are trusted only when they can produce a number.

None of this is an argument for abandoning measurement. Without data, failures go unnoticed and resources are wasted. The lesson is rather that numbers should inform judgement, not replace it. Measures work best when there are several of them, when they are used to ask questions rather than to hand out rewards and punishments, and when the people being measured are trusted to explain what the figures cannot.

title: The Final Bell
text:
On the morning of his retirement, Master Karim arrived at the school half an hour early, as he had done every working day for thirty-one years. The gate was still locked. He waited beside it with his cloth bag on his shoulder, watching the milk carts pass and the sweeper moving his broom in slow arcs across the road, and he found that he could not remember a single morning on which he had noticed these things before.

The day itself was much like any other. He taught the same lesson on fractions to the same restless class, and the same boy at the back asked, as someone always did, what use fractions would ever be to him. Master Karim gave the answer he had given for three decades, about dividing bread and land and inheritance, and the boy looked no more convinced than his predecessors. Only at the end of the lesson, when the class rose together and one of the girls stepped forward with a garland of marigolds, did he realise that they had known all along.

There were speeches in the afternoon. The headmistress spoke of dedication, and an official from the education office, who had never visited the school before, spoke at length about the importance of teachers. Master Karim listened politely and heard very little. He was thinking of the boys and girls, now grown men and women, who had passed through his classroom; of the few who had written to him, and the many who had not, and of how impossible it was to know what, if anything, he had given them.

When at last he walked out through the gate, the sweeper was resting under the neem tree. The man raised a hand in greeting, as though they were old acquaintances. Master Karim returned the gesture and, for the first time that day, smiled without effort.

title: History in the Kitchen Cupboard
text:
The new exhibition at the city museum takes an unusual approach to history. Instead of the swords, crowns and treaties that fill most historical displays, it presents the ordinary objects of daily life across roughly two centuries: cooking pots, school slates, ration cards, sewing machines, radios and the first plastic buckets that replaced brass and clay in countless kitchens. The premise is that the texture of the past is found as much in what people used as in what their rulers did.

For the most part, the premise is triumphantly vindicated. The objects are arranged not by date but by activity, so that a visitor moves through rooms devoted to cooking, washing, learning, travelling and keeping in touch. Within each room, the older objects stand beside their successors, and the effect is to make change visible in a way that no chart could. A worn wooden writing board placed next to a cheap mobile telephone says more about the transformation of communication than a page of explanation.

The labels, mercifully brief, are written in plain language and often quote the recollections of people who used the objects. These voices give the exhibition much of its warmth. One elderly woman remembers the day her family’s first radio arrived, and how the neighbours crowded into the courtyard to listen.

If the exhibition has a weakness, it is a tendency towards nostalgia. The hardships that many of these objects represent, such as the hours spent fetching water or the scarcity recorded in ration cards, are acknowledged but seldom dwelt upon, and the overall mood is one of affectionate remembrance rather than critical inquiry. Visitors may leave feeling that the past was simpler and kinder than it was.

That reservation aside, this is an intelligent and humane exhibition, and one that should be seen by anyone who believes that history is only about the powerful.

title: Managing What Belongs to All
text:
Imagine a pasture open to every herder in a village. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding one more animal to his flock, while the cost of the extra grazing, a slightly poorer pasture, is shared among everyone. Acting sensibly on his own account, each herder adds animals, and the pasture is eventually ruined for all. This simple story has been told many times to explain why shared resources, from fisheries to forests to the atmosphere, are so often overused.

The lesson commonly drawn from the story is that shared resources must either be divided into private property or placed under the firm control of the state. Both solutions have their successes. Yet careful research into how communities actually manage common resources has revealed a third possibility that the simple story overlooks. Around the world, villages have managed irrigation channels, grazing lands and fishing grounds collectively for generations, without either privatising them or handing them to distant officials.

Such arrangements tend to share certain features. The boundaries of the resource and the group entitled to use it are clearly defined. The users themselves take part in making the rules, which are therefore suited to local conditions and widely regarded as fair. Compliance is monitored, often by the users themselves, and those who break the rules face penalties that begin mildly and increase with repeated offences. Disputes can be settled quickly and cheaply, and outside authorities respect the community’s right to organise its own affairs.

The practical implication for policy is significant. Governments that sweep aside functioning local institutions in the name of modernisation may destroy arrangements that worked, replacing them with rules that are poorly enforced and resented. A wiser course is to recognise and support community management where it exists, while stepping in where local institutions have broken down or where a resource is too large for any single community to govern.

subject: English
q: Which of the following best summarises the author’s argument?
o: All performance measurement should be abolished
Hospitals and schools routinely falsify their data
Numbers are always more reliable than professional judgement
Measurement is useful but becomes harmful when numbers replace judgement
explanation: The author shows how targets can distort institutions but concludes that measurement should not be abandoned: ‘numbers should inform judgement, not replace it’.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, a school judged solely by pass rates may:
o: discourage weaker pupils from sitting examinations
move pupils into corridors to save time
stop recording attendance
hire extra teachers for weaker pupils
explanation: The second paragraph says such a school ‘may discourage weaker pupils from sitting examinations at all’, which raises the pass rate without improving teaching.

subject: English
q: The examples of the hospital and the school are used to show that:
o: hospitals are worse managed than schools
targets always reduce waiting times
a figure can improve while the reality behind it does not
most professionals are dishonest
explanation: The author sums up both examples: ‘the figure improves while the reality it was supposed to reflect stays the same or grows worse’.

subject: English
q: The word ‘subtler’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: more severe
more recent
less obvious
less important
explanation: The ‘subtler cost’ is the quiet neglect of uncounted qualities such as kindness and trust — a harm harder to see than the gaming of targets, not necessarily a smaller one.

subject: English
q: The passage suggests that qualities such as a nurse’s kindness are neglected because:
o: institutions tend to value only what appears in performance tables
nurses are no longer trained to be kind
kindness cannot be taught
patients do not appreciate it
explanation: The third paragraph notes that such qualities do not appear in performance tables and that ‘in institutions that value only what appears there, they are gradually neglected’.

subject: English
q: Which of the following practices would the author most likely support?
o: Linking every employee’s pay to a single target
Ending all collection of performance data
Publishing league tables based only on examination results
Using several measures to prompt questions, while letting staff explain the figures
explanation: The last paragraph says measures work best when there are several, when they are used to ask questions rather than distribute rewards and punishments, and when those measured may explain the figures.

subject: English
q: The passage is mainly about:
o: the difficulty of teaching fractions to children
a teacher’s experiences and reflections on the day he retires
a quarrel between a teacher and his headmistress
the reform of a village school
explanation: The narrative follows Master Karim from his early arrival on his retirement day through his last lesson and the farewell speeches to his departure.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, what did Master Karim teach on his last day?
o: A lesson on fractions
A lesson on the law of inheritance
A lesson on the history of the school
A lesson on letter writing
explanation: The second paragraph says he ‘taught the same lesson on fractions to the same restless class’; inheritance appears only in his explanation of why fractions matter.

subject: English
q: The remark that he ‘could not remember a single morning on which he had noticed these things before’ suggests that:
o: he had usually arrived late in the past
the milk carts and the sweeper were new to the area
the end of his career made him newly attentive to familiar surroundings
his memory had been failing for some years
explanation: He had arrived early every day for thirty-one years, so the scenes were not new; it is the sense of an ending that makes him notice them for the first time.

subject: English
q: When the girl stepped forward with a garland, Master Karim realised that the class:
o: had forgotten about his retirement
had known all along that it was his last day
had finally understood the lesson on fractions
had been told to behave well by the headmistress
explanation: The garland is a farewell gift; the class had behaved as usual all through the lesson, so he realises only then that they ‘had known all along’ it was his final day.

subject: English
q: The word ‘predecessors’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: his present classmates
his former teachers
his ancestors
those who had come before him
explanation: The boy looked no more convinced than ‘his predecessors’ — the earlier pupils who, year after year, had asked the same question and heard the same answer.

subject: English
q: The description of the official from the education office is best described as:
o: deeply admiring
gently ironic
openly angry
entirely neutral
explanation: An official ‘who had never visited the school before’ speaks ‘at length about the importance of teachers’; the contrast between his words and his neglect is quietly ironic.

subject: English
q: The primary purpose of the passage is to:
o: describe the history of the city museum
argue that museums should display only weapons and treaties
explain how early radios were manufactured
review a museum exhibition about the everyday objects of the past
explanation: The passage describes the exhibition’s premise and arrangement, praises its labels, notes a weakness and gives an overall verdict — the elements of a review.

subject: English
q: According to the reviewer, how are the objects in the exhibition arranged?
o: By activity, such as cooking, washing and travelling
In strict order of date
By the region they came from
By their value and rarity
explanation: The second paragraph says the objects ‘are arranged not by date but by activity’, with rooms devoted to cooking, washing, learning, travelling and keeping in touch.

subject: English
q: The word ‘vindicated’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: strongly challenged
widely advertised
shown to be justified
quietly abandoned
explanation: The reviewer goes on to show that the exhibition’s premise works, so a premise ‘triumphantly vindicated’ is one proved right.

subject: English
q: What weakness does the reviewer find in the exhibition?
o: Its labels are too long and technical
It contains too few objects
It presents the past too nostalgically
It concentrates too heavily on rulers
explanation: The fourth paragraph names ‘a tendency towards nostalgia’: hardships are acknowledged but seldom dwelt upon; the labels are praised as ‘mercifully brief’.

subject: English
q: The writing board placed next to a mobile telephone is mentioned to illustrate that:
o: setting old and new objects side by side makes historical change vivid
writing boards were more durable than telephones
the exhibition is arranged by date
communication has changed very little
explanation: The example follows the point that pairing older objects with their successors ‘make[s] change visible in a way that no chart could’.

subject: English
q: The reviewer’s closing remark suggests that the exhibition would be especially valuable for people who:
o: already know a great deal about domestic life
dislike visiting museums
are interested chiefly in modern technology
think of history mainly as the story of rulers and great events
explanation: The reviewer recommends it to ‘anyone who believes that history is only about the powerful’, since its premise is that the past lies as much in ordinary objects as in what rulers did.

subject: English
q: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
o: Shared resources must always be turned into private property
Communities can manage shared resources successfully, and policy should support them where they do
The state is the only reliable manager of natural resources
Herders are to blame for the destruction of pastures
explanation: The passage uses the pasture story only to introduce ‘a third possibility’ — collective management by users — and ends by urging governments to recognise and support it.

subject: English
q: In the story of the pasture, why does each herder keep adding animals?
o: He gains the full benefit of an extra animal while its cost is shared by all
The village council orders him to do so
He wishes to ruin the pasture for his neighbours
The pasture has unlimited grass
explanation: The first paragraph says each herder ‘gains the full benefit of adding one more animal’, while the cost of poorer grazing ‘is shared among everyone’.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, penalties in successful community arrangements typically:
o: are imposed only by outside authorities
are severe from the first offence
begin mildly and increase with repeated offences
are hardly ever applied
explanation: The third paragraph says rule-breakers ‘face penalties that begin mildly and increase with repeated offences’.

subject: English
q: The word ‘compliance’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: praise for good work
obedience to the rules
complaint about unfairness
completion of a task
explanation: ‘Compliance is monitored’ in a passage about rules and penalties for breaking them, so it means whether users obey the rules.

subject: English
q: The author suggests that the ‘simple story’ is incomplete because it:
o: exaggerates the value of private property
wrongly assumes that herders act sensibly
applies only to fisheries and forests
overlooks the possibility of successful management by the users themselves
explanation: The second paragraph says research ‘has revealed a third possibility that the simple story overlooks’: communities managing resources collectively.

subject: English
q: The author would most likely oppose a government policy that:
o: helps a community settle water disputes quickly and cheaply
replaces a working village system of irrigation management with centrally imposed rules
regulates a resource too large for any single community
recognises a village’s right to set its own grazing rules
explanation: The final paragraph warns that sweeping aside ‘functioning local institutions’ destroys arrangements that worked; the other policies are ones the author endorses.
